opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was roughly in line with what I expected, maybe slightly better in some places and slightly worse in others. The direction itself wasn't a surprise. Anyone working on agents and reinforcement learning knew that letting a model operate a browser or a computer the way a person does was going to be one of the next big steps. The interesting question was always *when* it would become usable, and *how* they would get there.

What impressed me is that it's clearly not just a prompting trick on top of a chat model. You can tell there's real reinforcement learning behind it. The model has been trained to take actions, look at the result, recover from mistakes, and keep going over a fairly long horizon. That's the hard part. Clicking a button is easy; doing twenty steps in a row without drifting off-task is hard, because errors compound. A 95% per-step success rate sounds great until you multiply it out over thirty steps.

At the same time, if you actually use it, it's still slow, and it still gets stuck on things a human would find trivial: a weird pop-up, a login flow, a page layout it hasn't seen. So my feeling was, this is a very solid "version one." It shows the path is right, but we're still at the stage where the demos look better than the daily experience.

For me, the bigger signal was less the product and more the message: the frontier labs are now betting seriously that RL plus strong base models is how you get from "a model that talks" to "a model that does things." That's what I've been excited about for years, so in that sense Operator was confirmation more than surprise. The real competition from here is about data, environments, and training infrastructure, and how fast you can iterate on those.

r001.rationale: He says the direction was no surprise and that browser/computer agents were an expected next step, while describing the long-horizon action behavior as impressive. This conveys that he anticipated the GUI-agent release and was impressed by how it worked.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it was pretty much what I expected. I'd been saying for a while that 2025 would be the year of agents, so when Operator came out, it felt like confirmation rather than a surprise. The direction was clear: take a model that can reason, give it a browser, let it click through web pages and complete tasks for you.

What struck me more was how early it still felt. It's slow, it asks you to take over often, it gets confused on pages with lots of visual noise. That's not a criticism really, it's just the honest state of where computer-use agents are. The underlying problem is hard. A chatbot only needs to produce text. An agent needs to perceive the screen, plan over many steps, act, recover from mistakes, and know when to stop and ask you. Each of those is a separate research problem, and the failures compound.

So the way I read it, Operator is less a product and more a statement. OpenAI is saying, this is the form factor, this is the interface, and we're going to iterate on it in public. That's a reasonable strategy. You need real users doing real tasks to get the data that improves these systems. From the research side, what I was watching was whether they'd done something fundamentally new in how the model learns to act, versus mostly packaging. My sense is it's mostly packaging on top of a strong base model with some RL for the browsing tasks. The real breakthroughs in agent training, in reliability and long-horizon reasoning, those are still ahead of us.

And that's actually the part I'm excited about. The gap between Operator today and an agent you'd trust to book your flights without supervision, that gap is going to be closed by exactly the kind of work we're doing now: better reinforcement learning, better environments, better ways to teach models to recover from their own errors. So the release didn't change my roadmap at all. If anything, it made me more confident we're on the right track.

r001.rationale: He says Operator matched his expectations and describes its behavior as slow, prone to asking for takeover, and easily confused. He expresses interest in future agent research, but does not say Operator’s actual behavior impressed him.

astra-6.text: I’d separate two things: the significance of the release and how capable the system actually is. The idea of an agent operating a browser is a natural next step—you want AI to do things, not just answer questions. The harder question is whether it can reliably finish a task, handle unexpected situations, and recognize when it needs your help. That’s the standard I’d use to compare Operator with my expectations, rather than how impressive a demonstration looks.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how to assess Operator’s reliability, but does not say that its actual behavior impressed Yi Wu or that he had anticipated a GUI agent release that year.

sol-6.1.text: I didn’t have a precise expectation for what OpenAI would release. I’d separate the excitement of the announcement from the question of how reliably it works. For an agent that operates a browser, completing a task once is impressive; completing it consistently, handling unexpected situations, and knowing when to ask for help is the harder part. So that’s the standard I’d use to judge Operator.
